title: What Happens to a Bear's Body When It Sleeps All Winter
description: A black bear just walked into an Alaska hospital for Halloween candy, and bears across the U.S. are raiding towns before winter. Here's why: we count down five things that happen inside a bear's body during hibernation, from a 20-second heartbeat to the one that sounds impossible.

scenes.say: A bear can go seven months without eating, drinking, or peeing. Not once.

scenes.label: Up to 7 months
scenes.say: And right now, in October, bears everywhere are getting ready to do exactly that. Which is why they're acting so weird.

scenes.label: Five secrets
scenes.say: Okay, so here's the plan. Five things that happen inside a bear's body when it sleeps all winter. Each one stranger than the last.

scenes.label: Stay for #1
scenes.say: And stay to the very end. Because the last one sounds impossible, and it happens in the dark, in the middle of winter.

scenes.label: Last week, Alaska
scenes.say: But first, picture this. Last week in Alaska, a black bear walked into a hospital. Through the automatic doors.

scenes.label: Three visits
scenes.say: Staff walked it back out. It came back. And around nine thirty at night, it pried the doors open and came in a third time.

scenes.label: Halloween candy
scenes.say: What was it after? Food from a coffee stand. And a whole bucket of donated Halloween candy.

scenes.label: Hyperphagia
scenes.say: Biologists said the bear was in something called hyperphagia. That's a fancy word for one thing. Eating like crazy before winter.

scenes.label: A hard lesson
scenes.say: Sadly, it didn't end well for that bear. Officials said it had to be put down for public safety. And it's not the only one.

scenes.label: No berries
scenes.say: Across the U.S., bears are breaking into towns this fall. A late frost wiped out wild berries in several Mountain West states.

scenes.label: 294 vs 60-90
scenes.say: Colorado had to put down two hundred ninety-four bears by the end of August. A normal year? Sixty to ninety.

scenes.label: Easy food
scenes.say: Experts say the cause is almost always us. Open garbage, grills, bird feeders. To a starving bear, that's a buffet.

scenes.label: Under 1 a year
scenes.say: Here's the thing, though. Across North America, bears kill fewer than one person a year on average. They're not hunting us. They're hunting calories.

scenes.label: 20,000 calories
scenes.say: And how many calories? A black bear biologist in North Carolina says fall bears eat fifteen to twenty thousand calories a day.

scenes.label: Up to 10x
scenes.say: For comparison, the same bear eats about two to three and a half thousand calories at other times of year. That's up to ten times more.

scenes.label: 20 hours a day
scenes.say: They can spend up to twenty hours a day searching for food. Acorns, berries, nuts. And they can gain up to three pounds a day.

scenes.label: 700-900 lb
scenes.say: In Alaska, the big brown bears do it with salmon. An adult male averages seven to nine hundred pounds in summer.

scenes.label: 1,200 lb
scenes.say: By fall, the biggest males can hit about twelve hundred pounds. Some of them look like furry boulders with legs.

scenes.label: 2.3 million votes
scenes.say: So the whole internet watches. This year, more than two point three million people voted in Fat Bear Week at Katmai National Park.

scenes.label: Backpack wins
scenes.say: The winner? A big, easy-going male called Backpack, bear eighty-nine. He beat bear nine-ten by just over five thousand votes.

scenes.label: Like mother, like son
scenes.say: His mom, Holly, won Fat Bear Week before him. And as a cub, he survived a bad leg injury that healed.

scenes.label: Why all the fat?
scenes.say: But why do they need all that fat? Because what comes next would kill almost any other animal. Including you.

scenes.label: 55 beats/min
scenes.say: Okay, let's start the countdown. Number five. The heart. In summer, a black bear's heart beats about fifty-five times a minute. Pretty normal.

scenes.label: Down to 14
scenes.say: Scientists at the University of Alaska Fairbanks tracked hibernating black bears. In the den, the heart dropped to about fourteen beats a minute.

scenes.label: 20 seconds
scenes.say: And here's the creepy part. Sometimes there were twenty seconds between heartbeats. Twenty. Count that out loud for a second.

scenes.label: 1 breath a minute
scenes.say: Rangers at Katmai say their hibernating bears get down to around eight to ten beats a minute. And about one breath every minute.

scenes.label: For months
scenes.say: One breath. Every sixty seconds. For months. Try holding still that long and see how you feel.

scenes.label: The furnace
scenes.say: Okay, number four. And this one surprised the scientists themselves.

scenes.label: Near freezing
scenes.say: Small hibernators, like ground squirrels, cool their bodies down to nearly freezing. That's how they save energy.

scenes.label: Stays warm
scenes.say: Bears don't. Their body temperature only drops about five or six degrees Celsius. They stay above thirty-one degrees. Basically, warm.

scenes.label: -75% energy
scenes.say: But their metabolism still drops by about seventy-five percent. Normally, you'd need a much colder body to slow down that much.

scenes.label: Still a mystery
scenes.say: So bears found a way to turn their engine way down, without turning off the heat. Researchers still don't fully understand how.

scenes.label: Half speed in spring
scenes.say: And the weirdest bit? When they wake up in spring, their metabolism is still only about half of normal. It takes weeks to come back.

scenes.label: Half asleep
scenes.say: So a bear that just walked out of its den is basically still running at half speed. For weeks. Imagine waking up like that.

scenes.label: No bathroom
scenes.say: Number three. Now here's where it gets truly gross. And truly genius.

scenes.label: Nothing
scenes.say: For all those months in the den, a bear doesn't pee. It doesn't poop. It doesn't drink a single sip of water.

scenes.label: Where does it go?
scenes.say: So where does the waste go? Think about it. Your body makes urea every day. If it stays inside you, it turns toxic.

scenes.label: Waste into muscle
scenes.say: The bear's kidneys nearly shut down. And then the urea gets recycled, turned back into proteins that rebuild muscle and organs.

scenes.label: Fat = food + water
scenes.say: Its stored fat does double duty too. Burning fat makes water and energy. So the fat is the bear's food and its drink.

scenes.label: Up to 1/3 gone
scenes.say: Some bears burn more than four thousand calories a day this way. By spring, they can lose up to a third of their body weight.

scenes.label: Muscles intact
scenes.say: Some black bears lose up to half their weight in the den. But here's the twist. Healthy bears walk out without losing muscle or bone.

scenes.label: No damage
scenes.say: Months of lying still, and no weak muscles, no brittle bones. Their blood cholesterol is very high, and still no hardened arteries.

scenes.label: Just walks out
scenes.say: Think about that. Your body would scream after months in bed. A bear just shrugs, stretches, and walks out hungry.

scenes.label: The blood
scenes.say: Number two. And this is the one doctors are obsessed with.

scenes.label: Why no clots?
scenes.say: When people stay in bed for a long time, blood clots become a real danger. So why don't bears get them after months of lying still?

scenes.label: Science, 2023
scenes.say: In 2023, a team in Germany published the answer in the journal Science. They looked at the blood of hibernating brown bears.

scenes.label: 55x lower
scenes.say: They found a protein in the platelets called H S P forty-seven. In hibernating bears, it dropped fifty-five times lower than in summer.

scenes.label: Same in humans
scenes.say: Then the twist. They found the same switch in people who stayed in bed for three weeks, in a study run with NASA. And in pigs.

scenes.label: On, off switch
scenes.say: And bears have another trick. They get very fat and barely move, which in a human would look like diabetes. But bears switch it on and off.

scenes.label: 8 proteins
scenes.say: Scientists at Washington State University fed grizzlies honey water mid-hibernation. They found eight proteins that may control that switch. All eight exist in humans.

scenes.label: Flip the switch
scenes.say: The honey water matters. Interrupting hibernation like that helped scientists spot which proteins flip the bear back to normal.

scenes.label: Not a cure yet
scenes.say: No cure yet. That's lab research. But think about it. A sleeping grizzly might help millions of people one day.

scenes.label: The impossible one
scenes.say: Okay. Number one. The one I promised you. The one that sounds impossible.

scenes.label: Born in the den
scenes.say: In the middle of winter, deep in the den, a mother bear gives birth. Without eating a single bite for months.

scenes.label: Under 1/2 pound
scenes.say: Black bear cubs are tiny. Newborns often weigh less than half a pound. That's lighter than a can of soda.

scenes.label: Milk from fat
scenes.say: There can be one, two, or three of them. And the mother feeds them milk, made entirely from the fat she ate last fall.

scenes.label: +5 pounds
scenes.say: By April, when the family finally walks out, the cubs have gained about five pounds. All from her body.

scenes.label: Every bite counts
scenes.say: Nursing mothers lose even more weight than other bears. So every berry, every acorn, every bucket of Halloween candy suddenly makes sense.

scenes.label: Not a villain
scenes.say: That bear in the hospital wasn't being a villain. It was doing what bears have done forever. Just in the worst possible place.

scenes.label: Space travel?
scenes.say: And here's the last twist. The Alaska researchers say bear tricks could one day help medicine, and maybe even deep space travel.

scenes.label: A golden week
scenes.say: Picture an injured person slowed down like a bear until help arrives. One researcher hoped to stretch the golden hour into a golden day, or a golden week.

scenes.label: Which one got you?
scenes.say: So which one got you? The twenty-second heartbeat, the recycled pee, or the mom who gives birth without eating? Tell me in the comments.

scenes.label: Next time
scenes.say: And would you want to hibernate like a bear for seven months? Yes or no? I read every comment.

short.title: A Bear Goes 7 Months Without Peeing. How?
short.header: How bears survive winter without peeing
short.description: Hibernating black bears go 5-7 months without eating, drinking or peeing. Their kidneys nearly shut down and urea is recycled into protein. Sources: University of Alaska Fairbanks (Science, 2011), National Park Service Katmai.

scenes.say: A bear can go seven months without peeing. Not even once.
No food. No water. No bathroom. Scientists in Alaska tracked black bears through five to seven months of exactly that.
So where does all the waste go? Here's the trick. Its kidneys nearly shut down.
The urea, the stuff that would become pee, gets recycled into new protein. That protein helps keep its muscles strong.
Meanwhile, its heart slows from about fifty-five beats a minute to fourteen. Sometimes twenty seconds pass between beats.
It can lose up to a third of its weight. But in spring, healthy bears walk out without losing muscle or bone.
That's why bears eat like crazy every fall. So when a bear disappears for months this winter, remember. A bear
